[USER] User is interested in the history of street art and its perception over time in different societies.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The history of street art dates back to the early 20th century when graffiti was first introduced in cities such as New York and Philadelphia.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] In the 1960s, street art evolved as a form of protest during the civil rights movement and anti-war demonstrations.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] During the 1970s and 80s, street art became a form of self-expression for marginalized communities, including those living in poverty and people of color.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] The rise of hip-hop culture played a significant role in the development of street art as a form of expression.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] In the 1990s, street art gained recognition as a legitimate art form, with artists like Banksy, Shepard Fairey, and Keith Haring becoming well-known.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Street art is perceived differently in various societies; in some cultures, it is seen as vandalism, while in others, it is welcomed as public art.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Recently, street art has gained mainstream recognition and become a tourist attraction in cities like New York, Berlin, and Melbourne.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Controversy surrounds street art, with critics arguing it is not true art and is a form of destruction.  
[USER] User requests more information about famous street art pieces and their significance.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] "Balloon Girl" by Banksy symbolizes the fleeting nature of life and cherishing moments and people we love.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] "Obama Hope" by Shepard Fairey became an iconic symbol of Barack Obama's 2008 presidential campaign and is part of the Smithsonian's National Portrait Gallery.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] "The Scream" by Banksy comments on censorship and the suppression of free speech.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] "Flowers" by Keith Haring symbolizes joy and positivity despite the prevalence of AIDS in the 1980s.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] "Kissing Coppers" by Banksy comments on the hypocrisy of law enforcement officials.
